name: Liquid silicone injection

lead: Liquid silicone injection places free silicone oil into soft tissue to create lasting volume. Those who choose it want fuller lips, a more defined face or larger curves without implants, and it has been used by physicians (in small microdroplet amounts for lips and scars) and, widely, by unlicensed injectors.

Medical literature mostly documents the complications: granulomas, migration, infections and, with large volumes, silicone embolism syndrome in the lungs. The FDA says injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure, and a scoping review of illicit cosmetic injections found cases reported from 28 countries.

paras: The material is injected through a needle into the target area, either by a physician using medical-grade silicone in small amounts or by non-medical providers in so-called pumping parties or private settings. Results are visible immediately, and the volume is considered permanent because silicone is not absorbed. No technique, product or sourcing details are given here.

Reported harms include nodules and granulomas, chronic inflammation, skin changes, movement of the material to other body parts, infection, silicone embolism syndrome with breathing failure, and death. Problems can occur years after injection, even with medical-grade material in small amounts. Removal is difficult.

angle.text: Silicone adds volume where it is placed, producing an immediate and persistent change in lip, facial or body contour. The same permanence is why complications can appear long afterwards and are hard to reverse.

lead: Liquid silicone injection is the placement of free liquid silicone, a non-biodegradable polymer (polydimethylsiloxane), into soft tissue to add volume or fill depressions. People seek it for fuller lips, facial contouring, breast enlargement and buttock or hip augmentation, because it gives an immediate change in shape that stays in place [1][2].

Two very different uses exist. Physicians have used small amounts of medical-grade silicone for lip augmentation, perioral rejuvenation and scars, with one review describing about 40 years of technique development [3]. Separately, injection of industrial or non-medical silicone by unlicensed providers has been reported worldwide, notably among transgender women seeking body contouring and among people seeking buttock and thigh augmentation at lower cost, and it is linked to disfigurement, silicone embolism and death [2][4][5][6].

The US Food and Drug Administration states that injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure, including facial and body contouring [7]. Historians trace the practice to the 1940s and 1950s, to Las Vegas in the 1960s, and to a 1966 decision to classify it as a new drug, after which the manufacturer abandoned efforts to win approval [8][9]. This article describes the history, how it is used and what medical literature and regulators report; it does not describe technique or sourcing.

paras: Free liquid silicone differs from silicone gel breast implants or solid silicone implants because it is injected as a fluid and is not contained in a shell. It remains in the tissue and may provoke a foreign-body reaction.[10]
Cosmetic uses reported in the literature include lips, face, breasts, buttocks and legs.[1][3][1]

Peters and Fornasier's review of breast injection materials dates the story to 1943, when Dow Corning and Corning Glass formed a venture to develop silicones for wartime use. Liquid silicone became a popular breast augmentation method in the 1940s and 1950s, particularly industrial-grade products in postwar Japan, and added contaminants in some formulas worsened outcomes [8]. Dow Corning developed a first medical-grade fluid in 1960, marketed for soft-tissue use [8].

In the 1960s, physicians in Las Vegas injected silicone in large volumes into showgirls and others, in some cases without keeping records; two physicians were reported to have treated over 10,000 women in ten years [8]. The National Academies history estimates 12,000 to 40,000 Las Vegas women received injections before Nevada made it a felony in 1976, while Peters and Fornasier date the Nevada law to 1975 [8][9].

In 1966 the FDA classified silicone injections as a 'new drug' and authorised a limited study of Dow Corning's fluid by nine plastic surgeons and one dermatologist; the authors state Dow Corning then stopped pursuing approval because it could not prevent misuse [8]. In 1991 the FDA issued guidelines forbidding marketing of injectable silicone for aesthetic use, labelling it adulterated, and a 1992 announcement said physicians could no longer use it cosmetically without approval; by 1990 over 100,000 patients had reportedly received facial silicone injections [8]. Silicone oils approved in the 1990s and 2001 for retinal detachment were reported to have been misused for cosmetic injection [8].

sections.h: Use in cosmetic and gender-affirming contexts
paras: A 2024 scoping review of illicit cosmetic injections screened 629 abstracts and included 142 citations from 28 countries; it found that roughly half of patients whose gender identity was described were transgender.[4] Reviews of gender-affirming care note that silicone injections for soft-tissue contouring are a medically unapproved route used by some transgender women, and that facelift may later be needed to treat cheek ptosis caused by silicone injections.[11][12][2]

A review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics of North America describes medical-grade liquid silicone for lip augmentation and perioral defects, reporting techniques developed over 40 years and combination with electrosurgery and shave excision where relevant.[3] Medical-grade silicone has also been injected in non-cosmetic settings such as foot padding in diabetic neuropathy and urethral bulking, in controlled trials.[13][14][15]

A 2009 New York Times report republished by NBC News described illegal silicone injection as a cheap, fast alternative to cosmetic surgery, popular by word of mouth among some Latina and transgender women and often arranged in homes, motels or at 'pumping parties' [5]. It recounted the death of a 43-year-old New York woman from silicone embolism a day after an injection by an unlicensed provider; the medical examiner ruled it a homicide [5]. A city epidemiologist quoted there feared cases were under-reported because doctors were not required to report silicone poisoning and silicone is hard to see on X-rays or CT scans [5]. An emergency physician who treats transgender patients said silicone produces results far faster than hormone treatment, which can take years [5].

In 2011, HealthDay reported three cases of silicone embolism syndrome after buttock injections presented at an American College of Chest Physicians meeting: a woman who recovered after a hotel-party injection, one who recovered after hospital treatment, and a 22-year-old who died of right ventricular failure [6]. The treating specialist estimated mortality near 20% when the lungs are involved and close to 100% when the brain is involved; the president of the American Society of Plastic Surgeons linked the trend to economic hardship and said unlicensed injections are often non-sterile [6]. A 2024 scoping review of illicit injections found reports from 28 countries [4].

People who choose silicone say it offers permanent volume without surgery, a lower price than implants, and immediate results; an emergency physician quoted by the New York Times noted the speed relative to hormone therapy [5]. Providers of medical-grade silicone in small microdroplet amounts describe it as a stable lip and scar filler with long clinical experience [3][16].

Regulators and clinicians dispute that it is safe for aesthetic use: the FDA lists long-term pain, infection, scarring, permanent disfigurement, blood vessel blockage, stroke and death [7], and published case series describe late nodules, cellulitis and migration even after medical-grade, small-volume injection [17].

A 1975 JAMA series described migration, granulomatous hepatitis, hypopigmentation and death after silicone injections.[18] A 1996 series of 54 patients with problems after medical-grade silicone injection to the face and legs reported chronic cellulitis, nodules, foreign-body reactions and migration, often appearing many years later, even with good technique and small amounts.[17]

Silicone embolism syndrome, with breathlessness, fever, cough, haemoptysis and alveolar infiltrates, was reviewed in a 2005 case report comparing it with fat embolism.[19] Other reports describe late granuloma formation, pneumonitis in men injected subcutaneously, and an autoimmune-type picture after breast injection.[20][21][22] Imaging reviews note silicone migration after buttock injections.[1]

Peters and Fornasier report an average of about 9 years between injection and complications in breast cases, with painful or multiple lumps appearing from 2-3 years to 10-15 years afterwards, and migration documented decades later in one patient [8]. In a Vancouver series, 13 of 92 patients injected in 1966-1976 developed granulomas [8].

The FDA says injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure and lists long-term pain, infection, scarring, permanent disfigurement, blood-vessel blockage, stroke and death among the risks. The agency's approved fillers are other materials, and non-absorbable fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars.[7]

Removal of filler may require further procedures, and the FDA states that permanent fillers and non-hyaluronic acid fillers may be difficult or impossible to remove [7]. The FDA's page also advises that unapproved fillers bought online may be counterfeit [7].

Controlled data for cosmetic use are limited. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 28 diabetic neuropathic patients gave silicone injections in the foot and reported outcomes at two years, but this was for plantar padding, not appearance.[13][14] A pilot of emulsified silicone with cross-linked hyaluronic acid has been reported as a filler combination.[16] Most cosmetic evidence consists of case reports, case series and reviews of complications.[18][17][19]

lore.intro: Silicone injection is discussed in cosmetic-surgery, transgender-health and bodybuilding-adjacent communities mainly as a low-cost route to volume, and in medical literature as a source of late complications [4][5].
